title: Miss Universe Moscow: Trump’s 2013 Invitation to Putin
description_medium: Donald Trump’s business brought the Miss Universe pageant to Moscow in November 2013, in partnership with developer Aras Agalarov and his son Emin. Trump hoped Russian President Vladimir Putin would attend and wrote him a personal invitation, according to people familiar with the letter cited by The Washington Post. Putin did not meet Trump during the trip; Agalarov said Putin sent a friendly note and gift instead. The episode documents Trump’s business-driven outreach and attempted contact, not a political agreement or evidence of coordination.
description_long: The 2013 Miss Universe pageant offered Donald Trump a business opportunity in Russia and a chance to meet Vladimir Putin. Aras Agalarov, a billionaire Moscow developer, and his son Emin helped bring the event to Moscow. Trump publicly asked whether Putin would attend and, according to people familiar with the letter, sent a personal invitation in June. The Washington Post later reported that the letter’s delivery to Putin was unclear. The pageant went ahead in November, but Trump and Putin did not meet. Agalarov told the Post that Putin canceled a planned appearance at the last minute and instead sent a friendly letter and a Russian lacquered box. Trump told MSNBC in Moscow that Putin was interested in the event, while later accounts describe efforts to arrange a face-to-face meeting that did not happen. This documents business-linked outreach and a failed meeting attempt, not a political agreement or coordination.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The episode highlighted early business-driven outreach to authoritarian power centers.
corrected_wording.revised_claim: The reporting documents a business-linked invitation and failed effort to meet Putin; it does not establish a political agreement or coordination.

source_access_notes: Supplied Washington Post URL was not accessible during retrieval. Same-event Washington Post reporting was opened and reviewed; it describes the invitation, Agalarov partnership, and failed meeting.
rationale: Uses contemporary event reporting to replace broad interpretation with the documented business arrangement, invitation, and outcome.

title: Trump’s 2017 Travel Ban Triggers Airport Detentions and Court Intervention
description_medium: On January 27, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769, restricting travel from seven Muslim-majority countries and suspending refugee admissions. Its immediate rollout left travelers stranded at airports and sparked protests and confusion. On January 28, a federal judge issued a temporary nationwide order preventing deportation of people detained at U.S. airports under the ban, including travelers with valid visas. The ruling halted deportations for those affected; it did not invalidate the entire executive order. The order faced immediate legal challenges.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769 on January 27, 2017. It restricted entry from seven countries and paused refugee admissions. Because it took effect abruptly, travelers were kept off flights, stranded, or detained after arriving. Reuters reported confusion and protests at airports nationwide the next day. Civil-rights groups sued on behalf of people held despite valid visas. A federal judge in Brooklyn issued a temporary nationwide stay on January 28 barring deportation of people stranded in airports under the order. The ACLU described two lead plaintiffs detained at JFK, including an Iraqi man who had worked for the U.S. military. That initial ruling protected people already detained; it did not erase the travel restrictions or decide the full constitutional challenge. The abrupt rollout made airport detentions, protests, and emergency court action central to the controversy. The preserved account also says Acting Attorney General Sally Yates was fired after declining to defend the order; the cited reports do not address that episode, so it is omitted here.

corrected_wording.original_claim: The order was quickly met with federal injunctions blocking its enforcement.
corrected_wording.revised_claim: A federal judge temporarily barred deportation of people already stranded in airports; the ruling did not invalidate the entire executive order.

source_access_notes: The supplied New York Times link concerned the 2023 January 6 indictment and did not support this 2017 event. Opened same-event Reuters coverage and ACLU’s January 28, 2017 court update. The Sally Yates firing claim was not verified from these sources and is omitted from the repaired prose.
rationale: Corrects the scope of the first court order and uses focused same-event reporting. Excludes the unverified Yates claim from repaired prose.

title: Scott Pruitt Resigns After Ethics Investigations and Management Scandals
description_medium: EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt resigned on July 5, 2018, amid scrutiny over spending, ethics, and management. Reports examined first-class travel, a discounted condo lease from a lobbyist’s wife, and a $43,000 soundproof office phone booth. The Washington Post also reported that staff assisted with personal tasks, including housing and a potential job for his wife. AP and the Post described more than a dozen federal and congressional inquiries, not 43 established investigations. His resignation ended a 17-month tenure marked by deregulation efforts.
description_long: Scott Pruitt resigned as Environmental Protection Agency administrator on July 5, 2018, after a succession of ethics and management controversies. The Associated Press reported that the scrutiny included security spending, first-class flights, and his rental of a Washington condominium from the wife of an energy lobbyist at a below-market rate. The Washington Post also detailed a $43,000 soundproof phone booth in Pruitt’s office and reports that he enlisted staff to help with personal matters, including housing and a possible Chick-fil-A franchise for his wife. The inquiries were broad: AP and the Post described more than a dozen federal and congressional investigations into spending and management. That count is different from the original title’s claim of 43 open investigations, which the sources reviewed here do not substantiate. President Trump praised Pruitt and said there was no single final straw, while reporting described mounting controversy and pressure from White House officials. Pruitt’s departure came after about 17 months leading the EPA, where he had pursued the administration’s deregulation agenda. The documented record supports saying that investigations and scandals surrounded his resignation; it does not establish that every allegation was proven or that the probes found wrongdoing.

corrected_wording.original_claim: At least 43 federal investigations; brazen ethical violations forced Pruitt’s resignation.
corrected_wording.revised_claim: AP and the Washington Post reported more than a dozen federal and congressional inquiries amid ethics and management controversies; reporting does not establish 43 open investigations or prove every allegation.

source_access_notes: The supplied AP link was inaccessible. Opened same-event AP and Washington Post reports from July 2018. Both describe more than a dozen federal/congressional inquiries; neither supports a count of 43 open investigations.
rationale: Retains the central resignation event while correcting the unsupported investigation count and avoiding unsupported findings or causation.

title: EPA Proposes Repeal of the Clean Power Plan (October 2017)
description_medium: On October 10, 2017, EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt announced a proposal to repeal the Clean Power Plan, the Obama-era rule setting carbon-dioxide emission guidelines for existing power plants. The EPA said it believed the rule exceeded the agency’s statutory authority and began a public rulemaking process. Existing requirements remained while EPA considered comments. The final repeal came in 2019, so this entry concerns only the proposal.
description_long: The Clean Power Plan set emission guidelines for states limiting power-plant carbon dioxide. On October 10, 2017, EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt announced a proposal to repeal it, arguing the rule exceeded the agency’s statutory authority. EPA published the formal proposal six days later. This proposal did not immediately remove existing requirements. EPA records the final repeal in June 2019, with the Affordable Clean Energy rule as its replacement. Pruitt framed the proposal as ending the “war on coal.” EPA opened a notice-and-comment process and said it would continue technical analysis before a final action. The official timeline lists the proposal and repeal separately, showing the policy change unfolded over time. The sources document the procedural steps but do not quantify emissions effects from the October announcement. The timeline also dates the original Clean Power Plan rule to October 2015, placing Pruitt’s action two years later.

corrected_wording.original_claim: EPA Rolls Back Clean Power Plan
corrected_wording.revised_claim: EPA proposed repeal in October 2017; it finalized the repeal in June 2019.

source_access_notes: Opened EPA’s October 10, 2017 announcement and official rule-history page, which distinguishes the proposal from the June 2019 final repeal.
rationale: Preserves the 2017 event date while clarifying the proposal/final-rule distinction with EPA primary sources.

title: Trump Receives Coronavirus Warning, Then Privately Calls It Deadly
description_medium: On January 28, 2020, National Security Adviser Robert O’Brien warned President Donald Trump in an Oval Office briefing that coronavirus could become the biggest national-security threat of his presidency, according to The Washington Post’s account of Bob Woodward’s interviews and book. Deputy adviser Matthew Pottinger also described an emergency. Ten days later, Trump told Woodward the situation was more serious than he had said publicly. In March, Trump described it as deadly and said he wanted to play it down. The report describes one briefing, not repeated intelligence warnings.
description_long: A January 28, 2020 intelligence briefing brought the emerging coronavirus threat directly to President Donald Trump. The Washington Post reported that National Security Adviser Robert O’Brien warned that the outbreak could become the biggest national-security threat of Trump’s presidency. Deputy National Security Adviser Matthew Pottinger agreed, citing information from contacts in China and comparing the danger to the 1918 flu pandemic. The reporting came from Bob Woodward’s interviews and book. Ten days after the briefing, Trump privately told Woodward he believed the situation was far more serious than he had said publicly. In March, Trump described the virus as deadly and said he wanted to play it down to avoid panic. The report describes one briefing, not repeated intelligence warnings. The January warning and later private statements contrast with his public downplaying, though this source does not establish that the briefing alone shaped the response.

corrected_wording.original_claim: Trump was repeatedly briefed by intelligence agencies and chose to conceal the danger.
corrected_wording.revised_claim: The cited account describes one January 28 briefing by O’Brien and Pottinger, followed by private statements in February and March that contrasted with public downplaying.

source_access_notes: Opened the linked Washington Post report. It supports a January 28 briefing from O’Brien and Pottinger and private conversations with Woodward on February 7 and March 19; broader repeated-agency warning claims are not supported by this account.
rationale: Scopes the account to specific briefing and recorded statements without asserting an unverified pattern or unsupported causal conclusion.
